title: The Silent Woman
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of humility and recognizing one's limitations in spiritual practice, particularly when it comes to awakening others from deep states of meditation or personal growth. A traditional Koan story about Manjushri highlights this point, suggesting that even with great wisdom and effort, some individuals may remain unresponsive or "snared" by their own flaws. Nomon Tim Burnett invites the audience to welcome their own "messy selves" and explore themes such as jealousy, trying to impress others, and practicing restraint in daily life, encouraging a more authentic and compassionate approach to spiritual growth.

Every year for about eight weeks, January to March, we have a period that we define as a time for practice, which is funny because it's always a time for practice.

Mostly people only ever get to do it once: to be the head student for the practice period.
The Sino-Japanese is shuso, which actually means first seat.
They sit in the first seat in the zendo.

So I guess you get advanced to the first seat when you're shuso.
We don't do that so much, a little bit.
Anyway, the shuso becomes the focal point to support all of us, and then we all try to support that person.
It creates this great field of mutuality and support.
The shuso is also acting as a beginning teacher, sort of like a teacher under supervision.
They give a class and dharma talks.
A sweet part of the tradition is that the first talk they give is about their own life, their spiritual biography, which is always quite interesting and powerful and heartfelt.
A lot of what they do there is remind us of their humanity, and how nobody comes to this if there's not some suffering in there somewhere, right?
So that'll happen.
The other thing that's neat about it is that since we have it as a defined period, people take a little time and think about their intentions for the practice period.
Maybe you do a little less of something else to make more time or energy.
Maybe you take something up that you've been meaning to get to, something to study, something to work on in yourself.
Maybe you have all kinds of intentions and then you forget them all over the course of the time.
That's pretty normal, too, and great, also fine.
It's not a great way to get stuff done.
It's a way to focus more on practice.
So that'll start in the middle of January.
All the events are on the website now and you can sign up for them.
Hope you do.

It's just an artifact of our system.
We can't do a combined thing.
So you've got to poke away at the website for a couple of minutes there and pay a few small fees to help keep the thing afloat.
That said, you're welcome to do as much or as little of it as suits you.

The problem with trying to write something up that you've been doing for 30 years is you think everything is clear, but it probably isn't.
So I hope you all get to do that together, should we all be here by then.
There's something else.
Oh, it was a much smaller thing.
I won't be here next week.
Raeus and I are having a little getaway.
So we're lucky John's going to give the talk.
And Chris will be Doshi and giving Dokusan.
And maybe John can give practice discussion too, since we've got him in the high seat.
We hope he'll be here.
Then I'll give the talk the week after.
And then we're almost to Christmas, and we'll skip the Thursday between Christmas and New Year's, whatever day that is.
We'll take a bit of a holiday break from the Zendo.
So I'm going to share about that.
So anyway, lately I've been really into stories, telling stories, thinking about stories.
Maybe our life is nothing but stories anyway.
On Buddha's enlightenment day last Saturday, I told different stories of the Buddha's life, some of which are traditionally told, but we didn't really know.
I think that was interesting.
When I was thinking about stories of the Buddha to tell on Saturday, I had a bunch of things that I also thought about women who were left out of that story.
So I told a few of those stories on Sunday at Zen Alive.
I got to give talks all weekend.
Then thinking about women in Buddhism made me think about another story that I wanted to share tonight.
It's a traditional Koan story.
We haven't looked at Koans in a little while around here.
So let me say a little bit about these stories that are called Koan.
It's a two-character phrase that means public case, like an example of practice, an example of awakening.
They're usually short.
They're often a little cryptic, presumably on purpose.
They were the practice stories that were floating around in China in the 9th and 10th centuries, and they were written down and collected into books.
Mostly they're about teachers and monks, and the characters who are named we think are almost always real people.
But what exactly happened may or may not be what's told.
That's kind of true of our stories.
Uncle Ralph didn't really do that thing.
It's just your family has said it so long, it makes it have happened.
Or maybe something similar happened.
So Koans are also kind of like the family stories of the Zen tradition.

Sometimes they include mythical, mystical characters who are also a part of our tradition, which can be a little surprising at first, because you hear about Zen or you get into Zen and it sounds very practical and down-to-earth and grounded and just sitting.
Buddhism isn't a theistic religion all about the great god, a great god, right?
And Zen, maybe Zen's not even Buddhism, it's even more down-to-earth than that.
But actually Zen includes all kinds of mystical characters to inspire us and challenge us.
If we're resistant to mythology, or at least to that mythology, we can also think of them as psychological aspects of ourselves.
So tonight's story has one of the great Bodhisattvas, Manjushri, the great Bodhisattva of wisdom.
He's often depicted holding a sword that represents cutting away delusion, a very yang character.
But the reason I thought of this story is that it's one of the few traditional Koan stories that includes a female character.
It has a second mythical Bodhisattva.
There's no real reason for Bodhisattvas to be gendered anyway, but they tend to get translated with he and him.
And Chinese is often ambiguous about gender anyway, so we could probably just reinvent the whole thing if we wanted to, and we should.
So this story has a woman in it, which is quite rare for these traditional stories, sadly.

There's been a wonderful modern effort, and there are about a dozen great books, to find and rediscover and retell stories of great Buddhist women and women teachers, of which there were many, of course, like, of course.
But those stories were not in the traditional collections.
We're now creating new collections, as we should, as we should.

So this is from the most important collection in terms of how often it's studied in Japan, the Gateless Gate koan collection, Mumon Kon it's called in Japanese, Wumen Wan in Chinese, and it's a story about Manjushri and a woman.
So here's the story.
*Long ago, Manjushri went to a gathering of all the Buddhas.*
So we're in mythic territory immediately.
*Went to a gathering of all the Buddhas.
When he arrived, all the Buddhas had returned to their original dwelling places.
Only a young woman remained, seated near Shakyamuni,*
who's like our Buddha,
*deep in Samadhi.
So Manjushri asked the Buddha, why may this woman sit so near to you and I cannot?
Buddha told him, well, wake her up from her Samadhi and ask yourself.
So Manjushri walked around the woman three times, snapped his finger and put her in the palm of his hand.
And they both transported to heaven using transcendent energy,*
this translation says,
*in an attempt to awaken her.*
So it's getting very far out.
*But he couldn't awaken her.
She stayed deep in Samadhi.
The Buddha then said, even a hundred, even if a hundred Manjushri appeared, they would also not be able to awaken her.
Far down below is the Bodhisattva of delusive wisdom.
He will be able to awaken her from Samadhi.
They will be able to awaken her from Samadhi.
Immediately this Bodhisattva emerged from the earth and bowed to Buddha, who gave him the command to awaken the woman.
So Bodhisattva of delusive wisdom walked in front of the woman, snapped his fingers once.
And at this the woman woke from Samadhi, stood up from her seat and bowed.*
That's the story.
This is really mystical stuff.
Here it is again.
Without comment, I'll try not to interject, and then I'll make lots of comments.
*Long ago, Manjushri went to a gathering of all the Buddhas.
When he arrived, all the Buddhas had returned to their original dwelling places.
Only a young woman remained seated near Shakyamuni deep in Samadhi.
Manjushri asked the Buddha, why made this woman sit so near to you and I cannot?
The Buddha told him, wake her up from Samadhi and ask her yourself.

Manjushri walked around the woman three times and snapped his fingers, put her on the palm of his hand, transported her to heaven and used transcendent energy in an attempt to awaken her, but she would not awaken.
The Buddha then said, even a hundred Manjushri, even if a hundred Manjushri appeared, they would not be able to awaken her.
Far down below is the Bodhisattva of delusive wisdom.
He will be able to awaken her from Samadhi.

He walked in front of her, snapped his finger and the woman woke, stood and bowed.*
So as I mentioned, the main character here, Manjushri, is the Bodhisattva of wisdom, a very powerful figure in the tradition, very shiny, very brilliant, very wise.
In the Mahayana Sutras, he often has the last word.
Occasionally, a few very notable times, he doesn't, and those are studied and treasured.
One time he gets shown up by a layman and now he's being shown up by a woman.
But he's usually amazing and brilliant and very impressive.
Here he's presented in a much less flattering light.
And this Koan literature is such a treasure that way.
It's kind of weird and wonderful.
The creators of these stories, I think, were very serious about our awakened nature and really wanted to point some things out and encourage us to pay a lot more attention.
So these are serious stories of awakening, and there are lots of ways that they get studied.
At the same time, they were irreverent and loved to mess with us, turn things upside down.
They have a quality of a very serious joke, or joking and being completely serious.
So Manjushri, as is to be expected, gets to go to a great gathering of the Buddhas.
He's like their right hand person.
But right away we know something's wrong.
Something's up.
Because he gets there late and he misses the meeting.
All the other Buddhas have already left.
It says when he arrived, all the Buddhas had returned to their original dwelling place.
But Manjushri, in his consternation, looks around and sees that there's someone still here with the Buddha: *only a young woman remains seated near Shakyamuni deep in Samadhi.*
Samadhi has a couple of shades of meaning.
It's literally concentration, and there are all kinds of Samadhis, and there are processes and states at the same time.
So we can think of it as a deep, deep meditative state.

These are described in the traditional teachings, and there are some where you have this kind of thought but not that kind of thought, and no desire, and no awareness of the outside world, and different things happen.
And these do happen.
This isn't just mythology, this happens.
It can be a good thing, a very important, powerful experience of practice, or it can be a not so good thing, or probably a mix of both.
We had a very early member, John would remember this, I don't know if anybody else here would, very serious about meditation, very devoted, coming to everything.
At her first seven-day sesshin, a retreat at Samish, I think it was the end of the first day.

It's the evening, the bell rings to get up and do the final chanting.
Everybody else is up in a shot, they're tired, their knees hurt, and she's still sitting very, very still, very, very peaceful.
I noticed her, but I didn't think about it too much.
Then we chanted the refuges as we do today.
Pretty sure we chanted something.
Then everybody filed out, except a couple of us.
Norman was there, I was there, a few people.
And this woman is still there, still in deep samadhi or in something, wouldn't move.
It was like she didn't even see us or hear us.
So it's kind of wonderful and kind of creepy.
Eventually Norman went and gently touched her shoulder and spoke to her softly.
I never did ask him what he said or what that was about.
I meant to.
And then, like the story, she opened her eyes, smiled, bowed, got up and left, went to bed.

And really it's a wounded soul, but with a very powerful connection to practice.
So that's probably not what's going on here, but just to say that powerful samadhis happen.
Sometimes they're wholesome, sometimes there's something else going on or something else mixed in.
And maybe it was good for this person I'm remembering.
Maybe it was a beautiful and helpful experience for her, I'll never know.
I just remember the dysfunction that happened later.
But in this case, whatever is happening for the woman in her story, Manjushri is attracted to her and threatened by her, and he doesn't even address her, he addresses the Buddha.
Why is she sitting here?
What's the deal with this?
Why may this woman sit so near to you and I cannot?
So the Buddha tells him to take some responsibility, wake her up and ask yourself.
So Manjushri, being a very powerful character with a lot of personal power, digs into his deep bag of tricks as a great Bodhisattva and does all the things that are described.

Transporter to another place where everybody's awake.
